subject: computer-science
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on the CPU and the fetch-decode-execute cycle, then mark my answer against the CCEA spec.
promptWeak: Explain the CPU, von Neumann architecture and the fetch-decode-execute cycle for GCSE CCEA Computer Science simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the CPU?
options: To process instructions and carry out calculations
questions.explain: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the 'brain' of the computer; it fetches, decodes and executes program instructions.

questions.q: A key feature of the von Neumann architecture is that:
options: Program instructions and data are stored together in the same memory
Data and instructions are held in separate memories
It has no memory at all
questions.explain: In von Neumann architecture both program instructions and the data they use are stored together in the same main memory.

questions.q: Which CPU component performs arithmetic and logical operations?
questions.explain: The ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) carries out arithmetic (e.g. addition) and logical (e.g. comparison) operations.

questions.q: What is the role of the Control Unit (CU) in the CPU?
options: It permanently stores the operating system
It directs and coordinates the operation of the CPU
questions.explain: The Control Unit manages and coordinates the CPU's activities, controlling the flow of data and sending signals to fetch, decode and execute instructions.

questions.q: What are the three stages of the machine cycle, in order?
questions.explain: The CPU repeatedly fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it, then executes it. This is the fetch-decode-execute cycle.

questions.q: During the 'fetch' stage of the cycle, what happens?
options: The next instruction is copied from memory into the CPU
The result is written to the screen
questions.explain: In the fetch stage the next instruction is retrieved from main memory (RAM) and brought into the CPU ready to be decoded.

questions.q: What is a register in the CPU?
options: A very small, very fast temporary store inside the CPU
questions.explain: Registers are tiny, extremely fast storage locations inside the CPU that hold data and instructions currently being processed.

questions.q: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched?
questions.explain: The Program Counter (PC) holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched, and it increments after each fetch.

questions.q: What is a bus in a computer system?
options: A set of wires that carry data, addresses or control signals between components
questions.explain: A bus is a collection of parallel wires that transfers data, memory addresses or control signals between the CPU, memory and other components.

questions.q: Which bus carries the memory location that the CPU wants to read from or write to?
questions.explain: The address bus carries the memory address the CPU wishes to access; the data bus carries the actual data.

questions.q: Which statement about RAM is correct?
options: It is slower than a hard disk
It is read-only and cannot be changed
It is volatile and loses its contents when power is off
questions.explain: RAM (Random Access Memory) is volatile: it holds programs and data currently in use but loses everything when the power is switched off.

questions.q: What is a key property of ROM?
options: It is used as the main working memory
Its contents are lost on shutdown
It is non-volatile and normally read-only
questions.explain: ROM (Read Only Memory) is non-volatile and keeps its contents (such as boot-up instructions) even when the power is off.

questions.q: Which type of memory typically stores the instructions the computer needs to start up (boot)?
questions.explain: The boot/start-up instructions are held in ROM because they must not be lost when the computer is switched off.

questions.q: A computer runs slowly with many programs open. Adding more of which component would most directly help?
questions.explain: More RAM lets more programs and data stay in fast main memory at once, reducing slow disk swapping and improving responsiveness.

questions.q: What is the purpose of cache memory?
options: To provide very fast access to frequently used instructions and data
questions.explain: Cache is small, very fast memory close to the CPU that stores frequently used data/instructions so the CPU does not have to wait for slower RAM.

questions.q: Compared with main RAM, cache memory is:
questions.explain: Cache is much smaller but significantly faster than main RAM, which is why only the most-used data is kept there.

questions.q: Why does a computer need secondary storage?
options: To store programs and data permanently even when powered off
To carry data between the CPU and RAM
questions.explain: Secondary storage (e.g. hard drives, SSDs) provides non-volatile, long-term storage so files remain saved after the computer is switched off.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a solid state drive (SSD) over a magnetic hard disk drive (HDD)?
options: It has no moving parts and gives faster access
It is always cheaper per gigabyte
questions.explain: An SSD has no moving parts, so it is faster, quieter and more shock-resistant than an HDD, though usually more expensive per gigabyte.

questions.q: What does the clock speed of a CPU measure?
options: The number of instruction cycles it can perform per second
The size of the hard disk
questions.explain: Clock speed (measured in hertz, e.g. GHz) is the number of cycles the CPU performs each second; a higher clock speed usually means faster processing.

questions.q: Why can a dual-core CPU often outperform a single-core CPU at the same clock speed?
options: It can process more than one instruction stream at the same time
questions.explain: Multiple cores let the CPU carry out several tasks or instruction streams simultaneously, increasing overall processing throughput.
